description: TerraTwin: Earth Analog Atlas is a digital atlas that compares Earth's landscapes with potential exploration sites on the Moon and Mars. Using NASA data, satellite imagery, and scientific research, the project will analyze geological features, terrain, and environmental conditions, with a focus on Indonesia's volcanic landscapes. The goal is to support planetary research and future space exploration through accessible maps and visual comparisons.
summary: TerraTwin: Earth Analog Atlas is a web-based scientific prototype that helps researchers screen Earth locations as possible analogs for lunar and Martian exploration sites. Instead of claiming two places are “similar,” it starts with a research question, such as rover mobility testing, and guides users through choosing comparable parameters (slope, terrain roughness, elevation range), reviewing candidate Earth sites, and seeing what is and is not comparable. The prototype highlights Indonesian volcanic landscapes (Bromo, Ijen, Merapi) alongside international analogs such as Haughton Crater and the Atacama Desert. Each page labels its evidence type (qualitative, hypothesis, illustrative) and references source datasets such as SRTM, LRO/LOLA, and MOLA. TerraTwin matters because transparent, traceable analog selection reduces the risk of overstating how well Earth tests represent other worlds.
details:
What it does
TerraTwin: Earth Analog Atlas is a web-based scientific decision-support prototype. It helps researchers and mission trainers screen Earth locations that could serve as test sites for future Moon and Mars exploration. The focus is Indonesia’s volcanic landscapes (Bromo, Ijen, Merapi), compared with lunar targets such as Mare Frigoris. Instead of asking “does this look similar?”, TerraTwin asks “what evidence supports comparing these places, and where does the comparison break down?”

How it works
Users follow a guided Analog Finder: define the target world and purpose, choose comparison evidence (slope, roughness, elevation, surface material, temperature), review candidate sites, and inspect the results. Each candidate has an evidence panel showing data status, source context, observation date, measured parameters, comparison criteria, and a confidence explanation. The Compare page sets an Earth site against a Moon or Mars target. Every parameter is labelled as qualitative, not processed, or source-verified, and a research summary is generated for each pair. The Data Laboratory lists the NASA and USGS datasets referenced (such as LRO/LOLA and MOLA) with their processing status, and the Methodology page documents a five-step process: Define, Standardize, Compare, Interpret, Reproduce.

Benefits

  • Prevents visual resemblance from being mistaken for scientific equivalence.
  • Makes the strength of evidence visible for every candidate site.
  • Gives students and early-stage researchers a clear, reproducible starting point.
  • Highlights Indonesia as a source of analog research sites.

Intended impact
To make analog site selection more transparent and traceable, so that Earth-based testing for lunar and Martian missions starts from honest, documented evidence. The longer-term goal is to grow the prototype into a tool that compares real, processed terrain measurements.

Tools and technologies
React, Vite, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS for the interface. Figma AI assisted with UI/UX design and prototyping. Data references: NASA Earthdata, NASA Planetary Data System, USGS Astrogeology, and LRO/LOLA and MOLA elevation products. Imagery is credited individually (NASA, ESA, USGS, and photographers on Unsplash). Hardware: a MacBook Air. [Add any other tool you actually used, such as the hosting platform or an AI assistant.]

How it is creative
Most analog tools lead with similarity. TerraTwin leads with uncertainty. It treats the limits of each comparison as a feature: evidence status tags, a “what cannot be inferred” section, and a transparent descriptive filter rather than a hidden similarity score.

Factors considered

  • Scientific integrity: no fabricated data, and measured data kept separate from interpretation and placeholders.
  • Image provenance: every image is credited with its source, and none is labelled NASA imagery unless verified.
  • Honest scope: this is a prototype with catalogue references only. No live data pipeline or raster analysis is integrated yet, and the elevation and slope overlays are marked unavailable.
  • Environmental differences: gravity, atmosphere, radiation, and thermal cycling are listed as limits on any Earth-Moon comparison.
  • Feasibility: a solo beginner project, so it prioritizes clarity and traceability over feature count.
  • Independence: it is not an official NASA product.
